name: Marco Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. Tell me what a normal shift looks like as a lineworker.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew for the electricity company, and we build or repair power lines after checking the site, the isolation and each person’s task. My two-year technical diploma helps with the diagrams, but I trust a second pair of eyes at the pole more than a tidy screen. The pay is low for this trade, and with two school-age children and a mortgage I pick up callouts when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I would say the AI talk has run ahead of the wires. A quicker form may be fine, but we will still be out fixing a damaged line in the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not relaxed about money even if AI mostly fizzles. We have less than a month of expenses saved, my lineworker pay is low for the responsibility, and there are few similar jobs nearby. An AI plateau will not pay the mortgage on a team lead’s low lineworker wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the repair crew and take available callouts. This month I would cancel one paid family outing and put the freed money toward the mortgage payment; in the first year I would ask the union steward to raise the gap between team lead duties and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, as I was before you read the card. The electricity bill, mortgage and school costs do not become lighter because AI slows down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense gives way first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend cinema tickets would go first, about thirty in a month. I would keep the children’s school things and pay the mortgage before any outing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the steward to bring to management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring my team lead rota and pay slips so the steward can show the extra responsibility without a matching rate. A general speech about respect would not pay the house bill.

say: **AI** hype does not change the crew’s physical repair work much.
I would **still** ask for fair pay for team lead responsibility.
think: **Less** than one month of savings leaves the mortgage exposed even without major AI change.
**Few** nearby lineworker jobs make a missed callout or bad pay rate hard to escape.
do: **Keep** leading the crew and take available callouts.
**Cancel** the monthly cinema outing and put that amount toward the mortgage payment.
**Bring** rota and pay slips to the union steward for a pay discussion.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills before any major AI threat.
S0.quote: An AI plateau will not pay the mortgage on a team lead’s low lineworker wage.
fieldNote: His **baseline** distress comes from low trade pay and a cushion shorter than one month.
He **stays** on the line and seeks a union pay discussion, not a technology change.

steps.text: Keep crew lead shifts and take available power line callouts
Cancel monthly family cinema outing to cover mortgage costs
Bring rota and pay slips to union steward for pay discussion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that software can book a repair but cannot make a pole safe by itself. If planners are cut, our union needs to know who will answer when dispatch sends the wrong crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hands are still needed, but overtime and staffing may tighten when office work is automated. I cannot fill a pay gap from savings for long, and I have never used an AI tool to argue with a schedule. A line crew cannot isolate a dangerous span by sending a message to a dispatch inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a paper record of every late or incorrect dispatch order for three months and bring it to the union safety meeting. In the first year I would ask the steward to demand a named human dispatcher on complex faults, and I would stop paying for a second streaming service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a sharper edge than the first picture. I know how to repair a line; I do not know how to make a distant scheduler understand a dangerous delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes in your paper record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write the work order number, time the call came, the actual hazard and who corrected the instruction. I already keep site notes, so this adds one column.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a named dispatcher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crew needs someone who can answer when a damaged line crosses another service. I will not let a generic inbox decide whether we have the right isolation plan.

say: A **booking** system cannot replace a crew’s safety check at the pole.
I would **demand** human responsibility for complex dispatch decisions.
think: **Office** automation may reduce planners and squeeze overtime or staffing before robots reach the lines.
My **thin** savings leave little room for lost callout pay.
do: **Log** incorrect dispatch orders with hazard and correction for three months.
**Take** the record to the union safety meeting and seek a named dispatcher rule.
**Cancel** the second streaming subscription to protect the mortgage payment.
feel: **Anxious** about tighter staffing and slow correction of unsafe orders.
S1.quote: A line crew cannot isolate a dangerous span by sending a message to a dispatch inbox.
fieldNote: He **treats** an accountable dispatcher as part of field safety, not a preference for old paperwork.
His **small** spending cut reflects little financial slack rather than a large new savings plan.

steps.text: Log incorrect dispatch orders and corrections for three months
Bring records to union safety meeting for named dispatcher rule
Cancel second streaming subscription to cover household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that full thinking AI by 2028 may erase dispatch jobs quickly, and capable line robots around 2031 put field crews next. We need a written wage and safety agreement before the company buys equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If callouts dry up, we cannot cover the mortgage from less than a month of savings. I lead one of the strongest crews, but a robot rollout could still cut the hours that keep the family afloat, and few nearby firms are hiring lineworkers. I can lead a power line crew through a storm, but I cannot lead a mortgage through a missing pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would take our mortgage and school costs to a household budget with my partner and cut the paid sports channel. In the first year after 2028 I would ask the union to bargain for paid crew retraining and income protection, and I would seek a meeting about temporary mortgage relief if callout pay falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious; I would be lying if I called it exciting. I know how to lead people on a repair, but I do not have a spare year’s wages to wait out a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the mortgage provider for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our callout pay actually drops, I would ask whether a temporary lower payment is possible and what it would cost later. I would not agree without reading the full terms with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the crew about your own fear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them my hours are at risk too, even as the team lead. I would ask each person to bring the actual hours and skills they need protected to the union meeting.

say: I would **push** for a written wage and safety agreement before line robots arrive.
**Thinking** AI could reach dispatch first, with capable field robots around 2031.
think: A **loss** of callout hours would threaten our mortgage almost immediately.
**Being** a strong crew leader does not create nearby vacancies or a financial cushion.
do: **Review** mortgage and school costs with my partner and cancel paid sports channel.
**Ask** union to bargain for paid retraining and income protection after 2028.
**Seek** temporary mortgage relief only if callout pay actually falls.
feel: **Anxious** about likely lost income and little time or money to adapt.
S2.quote: I can lead a power line crew through a storm, but I cannot lead a mortgage through a missing pay packet.
fieldNote: His **team** lead skill does not compensate for low pay, thin savings and few nearby jobs.
He **asks** for group bargaining and conditional mortgage support rather than claiming he can self-fund training.

steps.text: Cancel paid sports channel and review mortgage with partner
Ask union to bargain for paid retraining and wage protection after 2028
Ask mortgage provider about temporary relief if callout pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years before thinking AI and three more before capable robots is time the company must use with crews, not just in a boardroom. I would ask for a paid route into line inspection, because somebody must check faults after a robot leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could do inspection; my diploma and crew lead work give me the basics. But I have never used AI tools and cannot pay for a course while the mortgage is tight, so a promise of future jobs is no help without paid time and an actual post. A line inspection certificate will not cover our mortgage unless the course is paid and the job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the union steward to obtain the inspection course requirements and wage rate in writing. If the company offers paid training and a posted inspection position at least matching my present income, I would enroll before 2031 and apply in the first year after thinking AI arrives; otherwise I would keep leading shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but I could see a narrow path. Five years is useful only if the training comes with wages I can take home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection post pays less than your current job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on line shifts and ask the steward to negotiate the rate. Our mortgage does not accept a new title as a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI inspection tool before training is funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a demonstration and ask questions, but I would not sign off on a tool I do not understand. Paid training is the condition for taking responsibility for it.

say: The **longer** runway should fund real crew inspection training before robots arrive around 2034.
I would **ask** the union for written course and wage terms.
think: My **diploma** may support inspection, but unpaid study is beyond our household budget.
A **future** job promise means little without a posted position and adequate salary.
do: **Ask** union steward for inspection course requirements and wages in writing.
**Enroll** before 2031 only if the company pays for training and posts suitable work.
**Apply** after 2031 if inspection pay at least matches present income.
feel: **Anxious** but able to see a path if training and wages are guaranteed.
S3.quote: A line inspection certificate will not cover our mortgage unless the course is paid and the job exists.
fieldNote: He would **learn** a new task, but only once the company pays for training and posts adequate work.
The **extra** years offer a conditional path, not relief from the household’s existing thin cushion.

steps.text: Ask union steward for written inspection course and wage terms
Enroll before 2031 if company pays course and posts adequate position
Apply after 2031 if inspection pay matches present income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years before thinking AI and three more before capable robots gives workers time to bargain and train younger crews properly. I would want the company to keep a paid human lead on each repair team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I might not want every storm climb, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or that I can retire. A paid safety lead post could suit my diploma and field judgement if its hours and wage are real. Ten years of warning cannot fill a lineworker’s empty savings account this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a proposal for paid human safety leads to the next union meeting and ask the company for a written pay scale this year. If a funded safety lead course and an opening at least matching my current wage appear, I would train before 2036 and apply when the opening is posted; until then I would keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the future, and still anxious about next month’s bills. The long warning helps me make a plan, but it does not put savings in the account today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a human lead if robots do the climb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lead must notice when a snapped crossarm changes the plan and stop the job before anyone is hurt. I would want that duty written into the job, not handed to whoever is nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your household before any robot arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A higher team lead rate now would let us build one full month of expenses. I would use any agreed pay rise first to fill that emergency account, rather than promise the children a new purchase.

say: A **decade** allows bargaining for paid human safety leads on line repair teams.
I would **keep** teaching field judgement even when capable robots climb around 2039.
think: A **safety** lead job could suit my diploma if wages and hours are real.
At **fifty-three** I cannot assume the mortgage is cleared or an early retirement is possible.
do: **Bring** paid safety lead proposal to the next union meeting.
**Train** before 2036 if a funded course and suitable post appear.
**Apply** for a safety lead vacancy only if its pay matches present income.
feel: **Uneasy** about future machines and still anxious over near-term bills.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning cannot fill a lineworker’s empty savings account this month.
fieldNote: His **long-range** role remains conditional on funded study, a real vacancy and pay.
His **thin** cushion keeps the mood anxious even in the slowest picture.

steps.text: Bring paid human safety lead proposal to union meeting
Train before 2036 if course is funded and suitable paid post appears
Apply for safety lead vacancy if pay matches present income

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because callout hours could fall before we can replace the income, and the robots follow around 2031. A written agreement on wages, paid training and human safety responsibility would help, along with honest notice if hours are going. The mortgage cannot wait while the company runs a long experiment. A power line company cannot ask my mortgage to wait while it runs a robot experiment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a team lead on low pay is meant to save when there is barely a month of cash behind the family. I would welcome a better rate now, before anybody promises a course later. My crew deserves safe work and a wage it can live on.

headlineQuote: A power line company cannot ask my mortgage to wait while it runs a robot experiment.
portrait: **Marco** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company team lead with a technical diploma and strong field judgement on damaged power lines.
His **lower-than-usual** pay, mortgage, two school-age children and savings below one month make ordinary bills a live worry.
**Few** nearby lineworker posts and a dislike of unfamiliar AI tools limit his ability to leave or self-fund training.
He **records** dispatch faults and asks his union for wages, safety rules and paid courses; any new role must pay enough.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 may cut callout hours before his family can replace wages, with hands-on robots following around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **written** wage agreement, paid training, human safety responsibility and early notice of lost hours would help him plan.
